Approval screen Five checks before "under one metre" becomes the answer Gold Coast's exemption is conditional. A low wall can still need assessment when the site adds load, proximity, infrastructure or a safety role. 01 Height and geometry Measure the retained height along the whole alignment, including steps and nearby terraces. 02 Surcharge Record driveways, buildings, pools, fill, traffic and steep ground above the proposed wall. 03 Separation Check the distance to buildings and other retaining walls; 1.5 metres is a key Gold Coast exemption condition. 04 Services and easements Locate known assets and review title information before deciding an alignment. 05 Fences and pools The combined fence-and-wall height and any pool-barrier function can change the pathway. Open guide → What is behind a properly drained wall The four parts of a wall drain, read in the order water meets them: from the soil behind the wall through to where the water is allowed to go. 1 Retained soil behind filter fabric The fabric lets water through but holds the fine soil back, so the drain behind the wall does not silt up and stop working. 2 Free-draining aggregate A gravel zone against the back of the wall gives water an easy path downwards instead of letting it build up and push against the wall. 3 Perforated ag pipe Sitting at the base of the aggregate, it collects the water and carries it sideways along the wall. It has to be laid to a fall, or it holds water instead of moving it. 4 A lawful point of discharge Where that water is legally allowed to end up. Worth confirming before backfill rather than after, because the first three parts only move the water - this is the part that finishes the job. Water has to finish somewhere An ag pipe without an outlet is only buried optimism. Wall drainage starts by tracing surface flow, seepage, irrigation and roofwater. It then needs filtration, drainage aggregate, a graded collection line and an outlet that does not concentrate water onto a neighbour. Ask the quote to name the aggregate, filter arrangement, pipe, cleanouts and discharge assumption. If no suitable connection is obvious, make investigation a preconstruction task. That is clearer than discovering a dead-end pipe after the wall is built. Explore the drainage guide Failure is a pattern Photograph the symptoms, not just the worst sleeper Wide site context helps distinguish drainage distress, post rotation, foundation movement and material decay. Include what sits above the wall and where water appears after rain. Lean or rotation Show the base, top and retained slope. Avoid loading or excavating near a visibly unstable wall. Bulging or opened joints Record whether movement sits between posts, through masonry or across the whole length. Staining or soil loss Trace wet areas, pipe outlets and washed fines; a visible leak may be the end of a larger water path.
